name: Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS) Ethnobotanical Archive
description: A curated, sourced registry of documented Southern African traditional plant knowledge — historical usage, honest research status, cautions, and the intellectual-property record of the communities who carried this knowledge.
disclaimer: This archive catalogues documented historical and traditional plant use, with named sources you can check. It is not medical advice: it cannot evaluate your health, diagnose any condition, prescribe any treatment, or recommend any dose. For illness, consult a qualified health professional or a registered traditional health practitioner; in an emergency call 112 (free from any South African mobile) or go to your nearest clinic. No plant in this archive is a proven cure for cancer, HIV, or COVID-19 — anyone selling that certainty is selling a scam.
guardrails: Catalogue, not clinic: entries document what is recorded in the ethnobotanical literature — never what you personally should take.
Every entry carries at least two named, checkable sources. Content that cannot be sourced does not ship.
Traditional use is reported as historical record, not as efficacy proof; the modern-research note says plainly what is and is not established.
Community knowledge is community property: entries record the intellectual-property and benefit-sharing status where one exists (the anti-biopiracy record).

entries.title: Lengana / Wildeals (African Wormwood)
entries.region: Widespread across South Africa, Lesotho and into tropical East Africa
entries.summary: One of the most widely documented traditional medicines in Southern Africa. Recorded use centres on respiratory complaints: leaves steamed as an inhalation or brewed as a tea for coughs, colds, chest congestion and fevers. It is a fixture of the written ethnobotanical record and of living practice from the Eastern Cape to Lesotho.
traditional_use: Steam inhalation of crushed leaves for blocked chest, coughs and colds — the most consistently recorded use across sources.
Leaf tea or infusion for fever and general respiratory discomfort.
Recorded topical and wash uses in some traditions.
entries.modern_research_note: Laboratory research exists, but clinical proof in humans is not established. Critically: Artemisia afra is not the same plant as Artemisia annua (the source of the antimalarial drug artemisinin) — published analyses find A. afra contains little to no artemisinin, so claims that lengana treats malaria or COVID-19 rest on a confusion of species, not on evidence.
cautions: The essential oil contains thujone; concentrated or prolonged use is not safe self-medication.
Persistent cough, fever or chest pain needs a clinic or doctor — TB and pneumonia are treatable but dangerous when self-managed.
entries.scam_alert: Lengana was heavily marketed with unproven 'cures COVID-19' claims. No plant in this archive is a proven cure for COVID-19, cancer or HIV. If a seller promises a cure, that promise is the product — walk away.
key_points: Among the best-documented respiratory remedies in the Southern African record.
Species confusion with A. annua (artemisinin) is the root of most exaggerated claims.
Traditional steam and tea use is the documented core — not miracle cures.
sources: Van Wyk, B.-E. & Gericke, N. (2000). People's Plants: A Guide to Useful Plants of Southern Africa. Briza Publications, Pretoria — Artemisia afra account.
Van Wyk, B.-E., Van Oudtshoorn, B. & Gericke, N. (2009, 2nd ed.). Medicinal Plants of South Africa. Briza Publications, Pretoria.
SANBI PlantZAfrica species account: Artemisia afra (pza.sanbi.org).

entries.title: Motsepelo / Cancer Bush (Kankerbos)
entries.region: Dry western regions of South Africa (Northern and Western Cape, Free State) and into Namibia
entries.summary: A recorded tonic plant of the Khoisan and later Cape settler traditions, used for general wellbeing, appetite, and digestive complaints. Modern laboratory research has explored immune-modulating and adaptogen-like properties, but human clinical evidence remains preliminary.
traditional_use: Bitter tonic infusions for general debility, appetite and digestive discomfort.
Recorded use as a general 'strengthening' remedy during illness recovery.
Topical washes recorded in some traditions.
entries.modern_research_note: The peer-reviewed review literature (notably van Wyk & Albrecht, 2008) records extensive laboratory and animal study — and is equally clear that robust human clinical trials are lacking. The common name 'cancer bush' reflects a traditional-use claim, not an established treatment: no regulatory body recognises Sutherlandia as a cancer therapy.
cautions: A clinical study found Sutherlandia reduced the bioavailability of the antiretroviral atazanavir — dangerous interactions with chronic medication are real; never combine without a doctor or pharmacist.
Anyone with cancer who uses it instead of oncology care is gambling with their life.
entries.scam_alert: This is the single most scam-abused plant in the archive: 'cancer bush cures cancer' is a sales pitch, not a finding. It costs people twice — their money, and the treatment time they lose. Report miracle-cure sellers to the SAHPRA and the National Consumer Commission.
key_points: Real tonic tradition, real laboratory research — and no established clinical treatment.
The vernacular name is a historical record, not a medical claim.
Documented interaction risk with antiretrovirals — mixing without professional guidance is dangerous.
sources: van Wyk, B.-E. & Albrecht, C. (2008). A review of the taxonomy, ethnobotany, chemistry and pharmacology of Sutherlandia frutescens. Journal of Ethnopharmacology 119: 620-629.
Van Wyk, B.-E., Van Oudtshoorn, B. & Gericke, N. (2009, 2nd ed.). Medicinal Plants of South Africa. Briza Publications, Pretoria.
SANBI PlantZAfrica species account: Sutherlandia frutescens (pza.sanbi.org).

entries.title: Devil's Claw (Sengaparile)
entries.region: Kalahari sands of Namibia, Botswana and the Northern Cape (South Africa)
entries.summary: A Kalahari plant whose secondary root tubers are among the best-evidenced African botanicals: European herbal monographs (ESCOP; formerly German Commission E) recognise devil's claw preparations for supportive treatment of painful, degenerative musculoskeletal conditions. San communities carried the knowledge; commercial harvest is now a major rural income — and a sustainability question.
traditional_use: Recorded San use of tuber preparations for pain, digestive complaints and during pregnancy recovery (documented uses vary by community).
Adopted into European herbal medicine from the mid-20th century onward.
entries.modern_research_note: Unusually for this archive, human clinical trials exist: reviews find moderate evidence of benefit for low-back pain and osteoarthritis, and ESCOP publishes an official monograph (Harpagophyti radix). That makes it the exception that proves the archive's rule: real evidence is specific, bounded and published — not a miracle.
cautions: May interact with anticoagulants (e.g. warfarin) and is cautioned against with stomach or duodenal ulcers and gallstones.
Wild-harvest pressure is a documented sustainability concern — buying certified-sustainable supply protects both the plant and the harvesters.
key_points: The archive's strongest evidence case: ESCOP monograph + human trials for joint and back pain.
Kalahari San knowledge at the root of a global export trade — benefit-sharing remains contested terrain.
'Evidence-based' means a specific, limited claim — not a cure-all.
sources: ESCOP (2019, 2nd ed. suppl.). Harpagophyti radix — Devil's claw root. European Scientific Cooperative on Phytotherapy Monographs, Exeter.
Van Wyk, B.-E. & Gericke, N. (2000). People's Plants: A Guide to Useful Plants of Southern Africa. Briza Publications, Pretoria — Harpagophytum procumbens account.
Van Wyk, B.-E., Van Oudtshoorn, B. & Gericke, N. (2009, 2nd ed.). Medicinal Plants of South Africa. Briza Publications, Pretoria.

entries.title: Bitter Aloe / Cape Aloe
entries.region: Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Western Cape and Free State (South Africa), Lesotho
entries.summary: Aloe ferox carries two distinct documented uses: the leaf gel applied to skin and burns (a living household tradition), and the dried leaf exudate — 'bitters' — a stimulant laxative recorded in pharmacopoeias and exported commercially for over a century. The two are different preparations with very different risk profiles.
traditional_use: Fresh leaf gel applied to burns, wounds and skin irritations — the household use.
Dried leaf exudate (aloe bitters) as a laxative and 'digestive cleanser'.
Recorded use as a general tonic in some Cape traditions.
entries.modern_research_note: The laxative action of anthraquinones (aloin) is pharmacologically established — which is exactly why regulators restrict it: the EU moved against hydroxyanthracene-derivative aloe preparations in food supplements in 2021 over genotoxicity concerns. Skin-healing claims for the gel are plausible and widely recorded, but formal clinical evidence is thinner than the marketing.
cautions: Bitters are a potent stimulant laxative: prolonged use causes electrolyte loss and dependence, and anthraquinone preparations are restricted in the EU supplement market.
Not for pregnancy, breastfeeding, or children.
A 'digestive cleanse' is marketing language, not physiology — the bowel cleans itself.
entries.scam_alert: Detox teas and 'aloe cleanse' programmes are a standing scam format: they sell you a laxative effect and call it health. Weight lost to a laxative is water and time, not fat.
key_points: Two preparations, two stories: skin gel (household tradition) vs bitters (restricted stimulant laxative).
Over a century of documented commercial tapping in the Eastern and Western Cape.
Established pharmacology cuts both ways — real effect, real restriction.
sources: Van Wyk, B.-E., Van Oudtshoorn, B. & Gericke, N. (2009, 2nd ed.). Medicinal Plants of South Africa. Briza Publications, Pretoria — Aloe ferox account.
SANBI PlantZAfrica species account: Aloe ferox (pza.sanbi.org).
Van Wyk, B.-E. & Gericke, N. (2000). People's Plants: A Guide to Useful Plants of Southern Africa. Briza Publications, Pretoria.

entries.title: Rooibos
entries.region: Cederberg and surrounds, Western Cape (South Africa) — grows wild nowhere else on Earth
entries.summary: A Khoisan tea tradition from the Cederberg that became a national drink and a global export — and the landmark case for protecting indigenous knowledge: in 2019 the rooibos industry signed a benefit-sharing agreement with the Khoi and San councils (a levy on the farm-gate price, paid into a community trust), and in 2021 'Rooibos/Red Bush' entered the EU register of protected designations of origin — the first African food product there.
traditional_use: Infusion drunk as an everyday tea by Khoisan communities of the Cederberg — the documented root of the entire industry.
Recorded use for digestive comfort and as a calming household tea.
entries.modern_research_note: Rooibos is caffeine-free and rich in unique polyphenols (aspalathin occurs in no other known plant). Laboratory and small human studies explore antioxidant, blood-sugar and cardiovascular angles — promising research, not proven treatment. As a tea it is widely regarded as safe; concentrated extracts are a different product from tea.
cautions: As tea: no significant cautions are documented at normal consumption.
Concentrated extracts and supplements are not 'just tea' — treat marketing claims accordingly.
key_points: The 2019 Khoi and San benefit-sharing agreement is the archive's flagship anti-biopiracy precedent: community knowledge, community payment.
EU protected-origin status (2021) — the name now belongs to the place and its people, by law.
Proof that IKS can be honoured economically, not just academically.
sources: Joubert, E. & de Beer, D. (2011). Rooibos (Aspalathus linearis) beyond the farm gate: from herbal tea to potential phytopharmaceutical. South African Journal of Botany 77: 869-886.

Department of Environmental Affairs / National Khoisan Council / San Council of South Africa / SA Rooibos Council (2019). Rooibos benefit-sharing agreement — public record, reported nationally (November 2019).
European Commission eAmbrosia register (2021): 'Rooibos / Red Bush' protected designation of origin entry.
SANBI PlantZAfrica species account: Aspalathus linearis (pza.sanbi.org).

entries.title: Buchu / Boegoe
entries.region: Fynbos of the Western Cape mountains (South Africa)
entries.summary: A Khoisan remedy recorded for urinary and stomach complaints — famously steeping leaves in brandy ('boegoe-brandewyn') — that entered colonial dispensaries and then world trade in the 19th century. Buchu later stood at the centre of one of South Africa's earliest bioprospecting benefit-sharing negotiations (2013), making it a twin case with rooibos in the intellectual-property record.
traditional_use: Infusions and brandy tinctures of the leaves for urinary tract and stomach complaints — the core documented use.
Leaves also recorded in vinegar washes and as a general household remedy.
entries.modern_research_note: Buchu is documented in herbal monograph literature as a traditional diuretic and urinary remedy; robust modern clinical trials are lacking. The essential oil's pulegone content is a real toxicity ceiling, so professional dosing limits exist in the markets where buchu is sold — another case where 'natural' does not mean 'harmless'.
cautions: Pulegone (in the essential oil) is hepatotoxic at high doses — concentrated buchu oil is not a home remedy.
Not advised in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
A urinary tract infection can ascend to the kidneys: burning, fever or back pain needs a clinic, and antibiotics when prescribed — buchu tea is not a substitute.
key_points: Khoisan knowledge that reached 19th-century European pharmacies — an early globalisation of IKS.
2013 bioprospecting benefit-sharing negotiations put buchu in South Africa's IP-protection record alongside rooibos.
Traditional diuretic reputation is documented; clinical proof is not — the archive says both.
sources: Van Wyk, B.-E., Van Oudtshoorn, B. & Gericke, N. (2009, 2nd ed.). Medicinal Plants of South Africa. Briza Publications, Pretoria — Agathosma betulina account.
SANBI PlantZAfrica species account: Agathosma betulina (pza.sanbi.org).
Van Wyk, B.-E. (2011). The potential of South African plants in the development of new medicinal products. South African Journal of Botany 77: 812-829.
